quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on fibre composition, blends and the vocabulary of core-spun stretch yarns.

questions.q: On what basis must a fabric label state its fibre content?
questions.explain: Fibre content is declared by weight. Thread numbers would ignore the different counts of warp and weft, and volume is never used on a label.

questions.q: A fabric has an all-cotton warp and a 65/35 cotton-polyester weft. Why is its cotton content well above 65 %?
options: Because the weft is lighter than the warp and the warp is 100 % cotton
Because polyester is lighter than cotton per fibre
Because the weft crimp is higher
Because polyester is counted at half weight
questions.explain: The warp carries more than half the fabric weight and is entirely cotton, so the fabric comes out about 83 % cotton. Fibre density and crimp play no part once the yarn weights are known.

questions.q: In a core-spun stretch yarn the elastane filament forms the core and cotton fibres are wrapped around it.
questions.explain: A core-spun yarn wraps a sheath of cotton around a central Lycra (elastane) filament; the filament gives the stretch, the cotton gives the handle.

questions.q: The draft applied to the Lycra filament during core spinning is typically about:
questions.explain: The lecture gives a draft of 3.9–4.2 on the Lycra. This stretching is why only a fraction of the filament's nominal denier appears per unit length of yarn.

questions.q: What is meant by residual shrinkage of the Lycra in the yarn?
options: The loss of Lycra as waste during spinning
The retraction of the stretched filament after spinning, which raises its denier in the yarn
The shrinkage of the cotton sheath on washing
The reduction in yarn count after sizing
questions.explain: After spinning the drafted filament pulls back a little (about 6 %), so each unit length of yarn now holds slightly more Lycra and its effective denier rises by the same percentage.

questions.q: The denier of a whole cotton yarn of count Ne is given by:
questions.explain: Denier is a direct system and Ne an indirect one, so they are inversely related: denier = 5315 ÷ Ne. Multiplying would make finer yarns heavier, which is backwards.

questions.q: A finer cotton yarn (higher Ne) has a higher denier.
questions.explain: Denier = 5315 ÷ Ne, so as Ne rises the denier falls. Ne 20 is 265.75 denier while Ne 30 is only 177.17 denier.

questions.q: A stretch sheeting is labelled 97 % cotton 3 % elastane although its weft yarn contains 6.65 % Lycra. The reason is that:
options: Half the Lycra is lost in finishing
The all-cotton warp forms roughly half the fabric weight and contains no Lycra
The draft halves the Lycra in the fabric
questions.explain: The Lycra sits only in the weft, which is about half the fabric weight, so 6.65 % of the weft becomes about 3.2 % of the whole fabric. The draft was already allowed for in the 6.65 %.

questions.q: In the composition worksheet, 'cotton share of this yarn' for the warp is 100 % and for the weft 65 %. The polyester share of the weft is therefore:
questions.explain: Each yarn's shares must add to 100 %, so a 65 % cotton weft is 35 % polyester. 17.1 % is the polyester share of the whole fabric, not of the weft yarn.

questions.q: To find the fibre composition of a fabric you first need the weight per yard of the warp and of the weft, as computed in Lecture 5.
questions.explain: The method apportions each yarn's weight per yard by its blend, so the warp and weft weights are the starting point of the whole calculation.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: Which formula applies, and which way the answer moves when a draft, a denier or a yarn weight changes.

questions.q: The Lycra denier present in a core-spun yarn is found from the filament denier D, the draft d and the residual shrinkage s as:
questions.explain: Drafting spreads the filament over d times its length, so only D ÷ d remains per unit length; the retraction after spinning then raises it by (1 + s). Multiplying by the draft would give more Lycra than was fed in.

questions.q: If the draft on the Lycra is raised from 3.9 to 4.2 with everything else unchanged, the Lycra percentage in the yarn will:
questions.explain: Lycra denier in the yarn is inversely proportional to the draft, so a higher draft leaves less elastane per unit length and the percentage falls.

questions.q: The Lycra percentage of a core-spun yarn is calculated as:
options: Lycra denier in the yarn ÷ yarn denier × 100
questions.explain: Both figures are weights per fixed length, so their ratio is the weight fraction of Lycra. The yarn denier itself is 5315 ÷ Ne, which must be worked out first.

questions.q: Keeping the same 70-denier filament and draft, a coarser core-spun yarn (lower Ne) will have a lower Lycra percentage.
questions.explain: The Lycra denier stays the same while the yarn denier (5315 ÷ Ne) rises for a coarser yarn, so the Lycra fraction falls. Compare 6.65 % at Ne 20 with a higher figure at Ne 30 for the same filament.

questions.q: The cotton weight in the weft is found as:
options: Weft weight per yard × cotton share of the weft
Weft weight per yard ÷ cotton share of the weft
Warp weight per yard × cotton share of the weft
Weft weight per yard × cotton share of the fabric
questions.explain: Each yarn's weight is multiplied by its own blend share: 0.2363 lb × 0.65 = 0.1536 lb of cotton in the weft. Dividing by the share would inflate the weight.

questions.q: Fabric cotton percentage is calculated as:
options: (warp cotton + weft cotton) ÷ (warp weight + weft weight) × 100
questions.explain: Total cotton weight over total fabric weight gives the label percentage. Averaging the two yarns' shares (option 3) would only be right if warp and weft weighed exactly the same.

questions.q: If the weft of a cotton-warp fabric is changed from 65/35 to 50/50 cotton-polyester, with the same yarn weights, the fabric cotton percentage will:
questions.explain: Less cotton in the weft means less cotton in the fabric; the percentage falls but stays well above 50 % because the all-cotton warp is unchanged.

questions.q: A residual shrinkage of 6 % on the Lycra raises the Lycra denier in the yarn by a factor of:
questions.explain: The retraction packs 6 % more filament into each unit length, so the denier is multiplied by (1 + 0.06) = 1.06. Using 0.94 would reduce it, the opposite of what retraction does.

questions.q: The yarn denier 5315 ÷ Ne already includes the Lycra, so it is used as the whole-yarn weight when working out the Lycra percentage.
questions.explain: The core-spun yarn is spun to its nominal count including the core, so 5315 ÷ Ne is the weight per 9,000 m of the complete yarn and the Lycra denier is a part of it.

questions.q: Doubling the width of the fabric, with warp and weft of the same blends and settings, changes the fibre composition percentage by:
options: Nothing — both yarn weights double together
questions.explain: Warp and weft weight per yard both scale with width, so their ratio and the blend percentages are unchanged. Composition is a ratio of weights, not an absolute amount.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Work through the composition and core-spun arithmetic with the lecture's figures and a few new ones.

questions.q: What is the denier of a whole yarn of count Ne 40? Use denier = 5315 ÷ Ne and answer to one decimal place.
A 40-denier Lycra filament is fed at a draft of 4.0 and has 6 % residual shrinkage. How much Lycra denier ends up in the yarn? Answer to two decimals.
questions.explain: 40 ÷ 4.0 = 10 denier after drafting; × 1.06 for retraction = 10.6 denier.

questions.q: A yarn of Ne 30 contains 10.6 denier of Lycra. What is the Lycra percentage of the yarn? Answer to two decimals.
Yarn B is Ne 20 with a 70-denier Lycra drafted 4.2× and 6 % residual shrinkage. Find the Lycra percentage of the yarn to two decimals.
The weft of a fabric weighs 0.2363 lb per yard and is 65/35 cotton-polyester. How many pounds of polyester per yard does the weft contribute? Answer to four decimals.
questions.explain: Polyester share is 35 %: 0.2363 × 0.35 = 0.0827 lb per yard.

questions.q: Warp weight is 0.2475 lb/yd (100 % cotton) and weft weight 0.2363 lb/yd (65 % cotton). What is the cotton percentage of the fabric to one decimal?
A fabric has an all-cotton warp of 0.26 lb/yd and a core-spun weft of 0.24 lb/yd containing 6.65 % Lycra. What is the Lycra percentage of the fabric? Answer to two decimals.
A spinner wants exactly 17.67 denier of Lycra in the yarn from a 70-denier filament, allowing 6 % residual shrinkage. What draft must be set? Answer to two decimals.
questions.explain: Rearranging Lycra denier = D ÷ draft × 1.06 gives draft = 70 × 1.06 ÷ 17.67 = 4.20.

questions.q: Warp weighs 0.20 lb/yd and is 50/50 cotton-polyester; weft weighs 0.15 lb/yd and is 100 % polyester. The fabric polyester content is about:
questions.explain: Polyester = 0.10 + 0.15 = 0.25 lb out of 0.35 lb = 71.4 %. Averaging the two shares (75 %) ignores the heavier warp.

questions.q: A yarn of Ne 20 (265.75 denier) contains 17.67 denier of Lycra. The cotton in the yarn is about:
questions.explain: Cotton = 100 − 6.65 = 93.35 %. The 96.8 % figure is the cotton content of the whole fabric once the all-cotton warp is added, not of the weft yarn alone.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Labelling, blending and stretch-yarn decisions as they arise in the mill and the merchandising office.

questions.q: A buyer wants a fabric labelled at least 80 % cotton. The weft is to be a 65/35 cotton-polyester yarn. Which warp will achieve this most surely?
options: A 100 % cotton warp heavier than the weft
A 50/50 warp of the same weight as the weft
questions.explain: With an all-cotton warp that outweighs the weft the fabric comes out about 83 % cotton. A 65/35 warp would give 65 % overall, and a 50/50 warp would give below 60 %.

questions.q: A stretch denim's weft is a core-spun yarn with 6.65 % Lycra. The marketing team wants to print '7 % elastane' on the garment label. What should the costing office say?
options: Agree — the yarn figure is close enough
Disagree — the fabric figure is about 3 %, because the all-cotton warp contains no Lycra
Disagree — the label must show the filament denier instead
questions.explain: The label states the composition of the whole fabric. The Lycra is only in the weft, which is about half the weight, so the fabric is roughly 97 % cotton 3 % elastane.

questions.q: A spinner changes the Lycra draft from 4.2 to 3.9 to get more stretch. What happens to the Lycra percentage in the yarn and to the elastane cost per kg of yarn?
questions.explain: A lower draft leaves more filament per unit length, so the Lycra share rises — and because Lycra is far dearer than cotton, the yarn cost per kg rises with it.

questions.q: If the lab reports the fabric as 85 % cotton while the costing sheet predicted 82.9 %, the most likely explanation is that the weft yarn's real blend or the yarn weights differ from the inputs used.
questions.explain: The calculation is exact for its inputs, so a gap between predicted and tested composition points to an input — the blend ratio of the weft or the warp/weft weights per yard — not to the method.

questions.q: A merchandiser needs the fibre composition of a 60×60 sheeting with a polyester-cotton warp and an all-cotton weft before the lab test is back. The quickest reliable route is to:
options: Assume the warp blend is the fabric blend
Compute warp and weft weight per yard from count, threads per inch and width, then apportion each by its blend
Weigh a swatch and divide by two
Use the supplier's yarn label percentages unchanged
questions.explain: The Lecture 5 weight-per-yard method gives both yarn weights; apportioning each by its blend gives the fabric composition. The warp blend alone ignores the all-cotton weft.

questions.q: The same 70-denier Lycra and 4.2 draft are used to spin Ne 20 and Ne 30 core-spun yarns. Which yarn will show the higher Lycra percentage?
options: Ne 30, because its own denier is smaller
Both the same, because the filament is the same
Neither — the draft cancels the difference
questions.explain: The Lycra denier is identical (17.67), but Ne 30 has a yarn denier of only 177.17 against 265.75 for Ne 20, so the fraction is higher in the finer yarn.

questions.q: A costing clerk computes the fabric Lycra content by multiplying the weft Lycra % by the weft's share of fabric weight. A colleague says the warp Lycra must be added. For a 100 % cotton warp the colleague is:
options: Wrong in effect — the warp term is zero, so the clerk's answer is already complete
Right — the warp absorbs some Lycra in sizing
Wrong — the warp share must be subtracted
questions.explain: In principle every yarn's Lycra is added, but a 100 % cotton warp contributes nothing, so the clerk's single term gives the full fabric figure.

questions.q: Reducing the residual shrinkage of the Lycra from 6 % to 3 % would slightly lower the Lycra percentage of the yarn.
questions.explain: Lycra denier in the yarn = filament denier ÷ draft × (1 + shrinkage), so a smaller retraction means slightly less elastane per unit length.

questions.q: Which of these would NOT change the computed fibre composition of a cotton-warp, blended-weft fabric?
questions.explain: Composition is a ratio of weights per yard, so order length is irrelevant. Weft count, blend and picks per inch all alter the weft's weight or blend and so the fabric percentage.

questions.q: To raise the fabric elastane from 3.2 % to about 4 % without changing the warp, the mill could:
options: Use a heavier Lycra filament (e.g. 105 denier) in the weft
questions.explain: A heavier filament puts more Lycra into each pick. Raising the draft or cutting picks per inch reduces the elastane in the fabric, and an all-cotton weft removes it entirely.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder two-step questions on composition and core-spun yarns, including the mistakes students most often make.

questions.q: Warp: 0.2475 lb/yd, 100 % cotton. Weft: 0.2363 lb/yd, core-spun with 6.65 % Lycra and the rest cotton. What is the cotton percentage of the fabric to one decimal?
A student computes the Lycra denier in a yarn as 70 × 4.2 × 1.06 = 311.6 and then gets a Lycra percentage above 100 %. The error is:
options: Multiplying by the draft instead of dividing
Forgetting to convert Ne to denier
questions.explain: Drafting spreads the filament out, so its denier in the yarn is 70 ÷ 4.2 = 16.67, not 70 × 4.2. The 1.06 factor is correct for 6 % retraction.

questions.q: A fabric must be labelled exactly 90 % cotton. The weft is 0.20 lb/yd of 100 % polyester. What must the weight of the all-cotton warp be, in lb/yd?
questions.explain: Cotton must be 90 % and polyester 10 %, so warp ÷ (warp + 0.20) = 0.9 → warp = 0.9 × 0.20 ÷ 0.1 = 1.8 lb/yd. A 90 % cotton label needs nine times the polyester weight in cotton.

questions.q: Two fabrics use the same 65/35 weft yarn. Fabric X has a warp heavier than its weft; fabric Y has a warp lighter than its weft. Both warps are all cotton. Which statement is right?
options: X has the higher cotton percentage
Y has the higher cotton percentage
questions.explain: The all-cotton warp pulls the fabric figure up from 65 % towards 100 %; the heavier the cotton warp relative to the weft, the higher the fabric's cotton percentage.

questions.q: Yarn A is Ne 30 and contains 10.98 denier of Lycra; yarn B is Ne 20 and contains 17.67 denier. By how many percentage points is yarn B's Lycra percentage higher than yarn A's? Answer to two decimals.
questions.explain: A: 10.98 ÷ 177.17 = 6.20 %; B: 17.67 ÷ 265.75 = 6.65 %; difference 0.45 points — B has more Lycra despite being the coarser yarn because its filament is much heavier.

questions.q: If the 6 % residual shrinkage were ignored, the Lycra percentage of yarn B (Ne 20, 70 denier, draft 4.2) would be under-estimated by about 0.4 percentage points.
questions.explain: Without shrinkage: 70 ÷ 4.2 = 16.67 denier → 16.67 ÷ 265.75 = 6.27 %; with it 6.65 %. The gap is 0.38 points, so the shrinkage is small but not negligible on a label.

questions.q: A fabric has a 65/35 cotton-polyester warp of 0.30 lb/yd and a 65/35 weft of 0.20 lb/yd. Its composition is:
options: It cannot be found without the counts
questions.explain: When every yarn has the same blend the fabric has that blend too, whatever the weights: 0.65 × 0.50 ÷ 0.50 = 65 %. The counts were already used to get the weights per yard.

questions.q: An Ne 24 core-spun yarn must contain 7.0 % Lycra. Allowing 6 % residual shrinkage and a draft of 4.0, what filament denier is needed? Answer to one decimal.
questions.explain: Yarn denier = 5315 ÷ 24 = 221.46; Lycra needed = 0.07 × 221.46 = 15.50 denier; filament = 15.50 × 4.0 ÷ 1.06 = 58.5 denier.

questions.q: The fabric cotton percentage came out as 82.9 % with a 0.2475 lb warp and 0.2363 lb weft. If the picks per inch are raised so the weft becomes 0.2600 lb/yd, the cotton percentage will:
questions.explain: More weft means more of the 65/35 yarn in the mix, pulling the fabric figure towards 65 %: (0.2475 + 0.169) ÷ 0.5075 = 82.1 %.

questions.q: Which combination gives the HIGHEST fabric elastane percentage, all with an all-cotton warp of equal weight to the weft?
questions.explain: Ne 30 with 70 denier at draft 4.2 gives 17.67 ÷ 177.17 = 9.97 % in the yarn, higher than Ne 20 at draft 3.9 (19.03 ÷ 265.75 = 7.16 %) or the 40-denier option (5.7 %). Fabric figures are half these since warp equals weft.
